title: Types, Coercion, and Scoping
description: JavaScript's quirky type system and the rise of let/const

concepts.title: Seven Primitives and One Object
concepts.contentHtml:
JavaScript has seven primitive types: string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, null, symbol. Everything else — arrays, functions, dates, regex — is an object.

The number type is a 64-bit IEEE 754 float. There are no separate integer and float types — 1 and 1.0 are the same value. This is why 0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3 is famously false (it's 0.30000000000000004). For exact integer arithmetic beyond 2⁵³, use bigint (1n, 123n).

undefined means "never assigned"; null means "deliberately empty." Both exist for historical reasons. typeof null returns 'object', a famous bug from JavaScript's first 10 days that can never be fixed without breaking the web. Use x == null to check for either undefined or null in one step.

concepts.title: == vs ===, and Type Coercion
concepts.contentHtml:
JavaScript's type coercion rules are the language's most-mocked feature. '5' + 3 === '53' (string concat). '5' - 3 === 2 (numeric coercion). [] + {} === '[object Object]'. {} + [] === 0 in some contexts. These rules are real, learnable, but counter-intuitive enough that the universal advice is just don't rely on them.

The == operator does coercion before comparison: '5' == 5 is true. The === operator ("strict equality") does no coercion: '5' === 5 is false. Modern JavaScript style guides essentially forbid ==; use === always. The one exception some advocate: x == null for null/undefined check.

The deeper lesson: JavaScript was designed in 10 days in 1995 and shipped before bad decisions could be reverted. Modern JS is a layer of better choices on top — "use strict", ===, let/const, optional chaining (?.), nullish coalescing (??) — preserving backward compat while encouraging sane code.
mathExpressions: \text{===: no coercion, deterministic} \quad \text{==: coerces both sides, full of surprises}

concepts.title: var, let, const, and Hoisting
concepts.contentHtml:
Old JavaScript had var, with two infamous behaviors: function scope (not block scope) and hoisting (var declarations move to the top of their scope, initialized to undefined). console.log(x); var x = 5; doesn't crash — it prints undefined.

ES6 (2015) introduced let and const: block-scoped, no surprise hoisting (technically hoisted to a "temporal dead zone" where access throws). const means the binding can't be reassigned; the value can still be mutated (const arr = []; arr.push(1) is valid).

Modern JavaScript style: const by default, let when reassignment is needed, var never. The result is code that behaves predictably: variables exist where you'd expect, accidental reassignment of a const throws a TypeError (and linters flag it before you run), scope is the curly braces you see.

title: Closures, Prototypes, and 'this'
description: Functions as first-class citizens, prototype-based OOP, and the binding rules

concepts.title: Closures: Functions Carry Their Scope
concepts.contentHtml:
A closure is a function that remembers the variables of the scope where it was defined, even after that scope has exited. JavaScript's first-class functions and lexical scoping make closures pervasive.

The classic example: function makeCounter() { let n = 0; return () => ++n; }. Each call to makeCounter() creates a fresh n; the returned arrow function closes over it. const c = makeCounter(); c(); c(); c(); returns 1, 2, 3. Even though makeCounter has returned, its local n persists because the closure holds a reference.

Closures power much of JavaScript: module patterns, callbacks with retained state, partial application, memoization. They also create the famous loop variable bug: with var, all closures in a loop captured the same variable. With let (block-scoped), each iteration gets a fresh binding — usually what you wanted.
mathExpressions: \text{closure: } f \text{ remembers } \text{scope}(f) \text{ even after scope exits}

concepts.title: Prototypes: OOP Without Classes (Originally)
concepts.contentHtml:
JavaScript's OOP is fundamentally prototype-based, not class-based. Each object has a hidden [[Prototype]] link to another object. Property lookups walk this prototype chain: if obj.method isn't found on obj, JavaScript checks obj's prototype, then that object's prototype, until null.

For decades, this was the primary OOP model. The class syntax (ES6, 2015) is sugar over the prototype mechanism — under the hood, class Foo still creates a function and sets up Foo.prototype. The class syntax is friendlier for developers from Java/C# backgrounds, but the prototype reality remains.

This affects how inheritance works. class B extends A sets B.prototype.[[Prototype]] = A.prototype. Methods defined on the prototype are shared by all instances; methods defined on the instance shadow them. Modern JavaScript usually uses class, but understanding prototypes still pays off when debugging or working with older codebases.

concepts.title: The 'this' Keyword: Binding Rules
concepts.contentHtml:
JavaScript's this is famously confusing because its value depends on how the function is called, not where it's defined. The four binding rules, in order of precedence:

new binding: new Foo() creates a new object and binds this to it. Explicit binding: fn.call(obj, ...), fn.apply(obj, ...), fn.bind(obj) set this directly. Implicit binding: obj.method() binds this to obj. Default binding: a plain fn() binds to undefined (in strict mode) or the global object.

Arrow functions are different: they don't have their own this. They inherit it from the enclosing scope. This is why arrow functions are perfect for callbacks where you want this to mean what it meant in the surrounding code: this.timer = setInterval(() => this.tick(), 1000). The arrow's this is the outer object, not the timer.

title: Async: Callbacks, Promises, async/await
description: The event loop, microtasks, and how JavaScript stays responsive

concepts.title: The Event Loop
concepts.contentHtml:
JavaScript is single-threaded. There is exactly one execution thread, and synchronous code runs to completion before anything else gets a turn. Yet a Node.js server handles 10,000 connections concurrently, and a browser stays responsive while loading megabytes. The trick is the event loop.

I/O operations (file reads, network requests, timers) are non-blocking. Calling fetch(url) doesn't pause the thread; it kicks off the request and returns immediately with a promise. When the response arrives, the runtime queues a callback to the event loop. The loop runs queued callbacks one at a time, never preempting.

Two queues: the task queue (timers, I/O) and the higher-priority microtask queue (promise callbacks, queueMicrotask). After each task, all pending microtasks drain before the next task runs. This is why Promise.resolve().then(...) runs before a setTimeout(..., 0) queued at the same moment.
mathExpressions: \text{event loop: drain microtasks; run one task; repeat}

concepts.title: Callbacks → Promises → async/await
concepts.contentHtml:
Early Node.js used callback-based async: fs.readFile(path, (err, data) => { ... }). Nesting many of these created the infamous callback hell — pyramid-shaped code that was painful to read and even harder to handle errors in.

ES6 introduced Promises. A promise is an object representing a future value: pending, fulfilled, or rejected. fetch(url).then(r => r.json()).then(data => ...).catch(handleErr). Chains stay flat. Errors propagate to the nearest catch. Promise.all runs many promises in parallel.

ES2017 added async/await: syntactic sugar over Promises. const data = await fetch(url).then(r => r.json()); looks synchronous but is async under the hood. try/catch works for errors. This is now the standard. Callback hell is essentially solved; entire codebases written in async/await read like sync code with awaits sprinkled in.

concepts.title: Concurrency Pitfalls and Patterns
concepts.contentHtml:
Common patterns: Promise.all resolves when all inputs resolve (or rejects on the first failure). Promise.allSettled waits for every promise regardless of outcome. Promise.race resolves with the first to finish. Promise.any resolves with the first success.

Pitfalls: unhandled rejections. A promise rejection without .catch or surrounding try/catch in async/await crashes the process in modern Node. Floating promises (calling an async function without awaiting) continue running but errors are silent. Sequential vs parallel: for (const url of urls) { await fetch(url) } is sequential; await Promise.all(urls.map(fetch)) is parallel. Big perf difference.

For long-lived async iteration, async iterators + for await of stream values one at a time. For CPU-bound work in browsers, Web Workers spawn separate threads. In Node, worker_threads. JavaScript's concurrency story is mature, expressive, and far better than people who last touched it in 2010 expect.

title: Modules, Bundlers, and the Ecosystem
description: ESM vs CommonJS, npm, and the JavaScript build pipeline

concepts.title: CommonJS vs ES Modules
concepts.contentHtml:
JavaScript famously had no module system for its first 15 years. Two competing systems emerged. CommonJS (CJS), used by Node.js: const x = require('mod'); module.exports = .... Synchronous, dynamic, server-friendly. ES Modules (ESM), the modern standard: import { x } from 'mod'; export .... Asynchronous, statically analyzable, browser-native.

For years the two ecosystems clashed. CJS files couldn't easily import ESM; ESM files needed file extensions, top-level await support, etc. Node now supports both, but interop remains tricky — particularly when a package exports both formats.

The trend is clearly toward ESM. Browsers natively support it. Modern bundlers default to it. Major libraries are dropping CJS support. New projects in 2025 should default to ESM ("type": "module" in package.json) unless you have a specific reason otherwise.

concepts.title: npm and the Package Ecosystem
concepts.contentHtml:
npm (Node Package Manager) is the registry and CLI. With over 2 million packages, it's the largest ecosystem of any language. npm install downloads packages into node_modules and records them in package.json. The package-lock.json pins exact versions for reproducibility.

Alternatives: yarn (Facebook's, with workspaces and zero-installs), pnpm (uses a content-addressed store to dedupe disk usage across projects), bun (an entirely new runtime + package manager, dramatically faster). Each has fans; npm remains the default for most projects.

The downsides of npm scale: massive node_modules directories ("heaviest object in the universe" memes), supply-chain risk (left-pad incident), version pinning fights. Modern best practices: lockfiles checked in, dependabot/renovate for updates, audit tools for vulnerabilities, minimal runtime dependencies.

concepts.title: Bundlers, Transpilers, and the Build Pipeline
concepts.contentHtml:
Browsers can't directly run TypeScript, JSX, modern import syntax with bare specifiers, or modular Sass. So a build pipeline transforms source code into browser-ready output: TypeScript → JavaScript via tsc; JSX → JavaScript via Babel or swc; many small ES modules → a bundle of optimized chunks via Webpack, Rollup, esbuild, Parcel, Vite.

The 2020s revolution is esbuild and swc: bundlers/transpilers in Go and Rust that are 10-100× faster than their JS-based predecessors. Vite uses esbuild for dev and Rollup for production, making the dev experience instant on most projects. Bun bundles everything: runtime, package manager, bundler, test runner.

Modern frontend tooling has consolidated. Vite for most projects; Next.js / Remix / SvelteKit for full-stack frameworks; Turbopack for huge codebases. The era of hand-rolling 200-line webpack configs is mercifully over.

title: TypeScript: Types Without the JavaScript Tax
description: Structural typing, generics, and why TS swallowed the JS world

concepts.title: Why TypeScript Won
concepts.contentHtml:
TypeScript (Microsoft, 2012) is JavaScript with a static type system. It compiles to plain JavaScript; types are erased at compile time. The pitch: catch bugs at edit time, get better IDE completion, document interfaces, refactor with confidence. By 2024, the majority of new JavaScript-ecosystem projects start in TypeScript.

The killer feature is structural typing. A type is just a description of what an object looks like; any object matching the description is compatible. No implements Foo declaration needed. This fits JavaScript's actual culture (duck typing, plain objects, late composition) far better than nominal type systems.

The success was driven by the gentle adoption path. You can sprinkle TS into a JS codebase, leave types loose with any, and tighten over time. tsc --strict turns the dial up. Combined with editor integration (VS Code is Microsoft's, after all), TypeScript made writing JavaScript dramatically more pleasant — without forcing developers to abandon the existing ecosystem.

concepts.title: Generics, Unions, and Discriminated Unions
concepts.contentHtml:
TypeScript's type system is among the most expressive in mainstream languages. Generics let you parameterize types: function first<T>(arr: T[]): T | undefined { return arr[0]; } works for any element type without losing type information.

Union types express "this is one of these": type Result = Success | Failure. Discriminated unions add a tag for safe pattern matching: type Shape = { kind: 'circle', r: number } | { kind: 'square', side: number }. Inside a switch (shape.kind), TypeScript narrows the type, and you get exhaustiveness checking.

Advanced features: conditional types (T extends U ? X : Y), mapped types ({ [K in keyof T]: ... }), template literal types, type predicates. The TS type system is itself Turing-complete, which is occasionally a feature and occasionally a horror. Library authors push these features hard; application developers rarely need them.
mathExpressions: \text{discriminated union: } \text{type } T = A | B \implies \text{exhaustive checks via tag}

concepts.title: Tooling, Frameworks, and the Future
concepts.contentHtml:
Modern frontend development is overwhelmingly TypeScript. React, Vue, Svelte, Solid, Angular all have first-class TS support. Backend frameworks: NestJS, tRPC, Hono, modern Express. Even Deno and Bun assume TypeScript by default.

The toolchain has caught up to the type system. tsc is reliable but slow on big projects. swc and esbuild handle TS-to-JS transformation 10-100× faster (without type checking — they just strip types). tsx and ts-node let you run TS directly. Editor integration via the TS Language Server is the gold standard for refactoring and autocomplete.

The biggest open question for TS is type-checking performance on huge codebases. Microsoft is rewriting the TypeScript compiler in Go (tsgo, 2025) for a 5-10× speedup. There's also growing interest in JSDoc-based typing for libraries that want types without a build step. TypeScript isn't going anywhere — its grip on the ecosystem is permanent. The next decade is about making it faster, more ergonomic, and removing the last papercuts.
